title: The Book of Psalms Timeline
sub: Five Books, One Song · From "Blessed Is the Man" to "Let Everything That Has Breath Praise Yah"
desc: Israel's own hymnbook and prayer book, organized into its traditional five books — David's own laments and battle-songs, the Korahite and Asaph collections, the pilgrim Songs of Ascent, and a final crescendo of unbroken praise. Quoted in the LSB, the only translation in this collection that renders the divine name directly as Yahweh.

eras.label: Era I · Psalms 1-2
eras.name: The Gateway Psalms: Two Ways, and God's Anointed King
eras.dates: The Psalter opens with a deliberately paired pair of gates — an untitled wisdom psalm contrasting the blessed man rooted like a tree against the wicked who blow away like chaff, followed by a royal, messianic psalm in which the nations rage against Yahweh's Anointed, a pairing later New Testament writers (Acts 4, Hebrews 1) read as pointing straight to Christ.

events.title: The Two Ways: the Blessed Man and the Wicked
events.detail: Untitled and unattributed, the Psalter's opening poem sets the whole book's moral framework in six verses — the blessed man who delights in Yahweh's law is like a tree planted by streams of water, while the wicked are merely chaff the wind drives away.

verses.text: How blessed is the man who does not walk in the counsel of the wicked... But his delight is in the law of Yahweh... And he will be like a tree firmly planted by streams of water, Which yields its fruit in its season.
For Yahweh knows the way of the righteous, But the way of the wicked will perish.

events.title: "Why Do the Nations Rage?" — God's Anointed King
events.detail: The nations conspire against Yahweh and "His Anointed" (Hebrew: Messiah), only to be met with laughter from heaven and the declaration of a royal decree — "You are My Son, Today I have begotten You" — language the book of Acts and the book of Hebrews apply directly to Jesus.

verses.text: "But as for Me, I have installed My King Upon Zion, My holy mountain." "I will surely tell of the decree of Yahweh: He said to Me, 'You are My Son, Today I have begotten You.'"
Kiss the Son, lest He become angry, and you perish in the way... How blessed are all who take refuge in Him!

eras.label: Era II · Psalms 3-7
eras.name: David's Early Morning Laments
eras.dates: A cluster of Davidic psalms — several tied by their superscriptions to fleeing Absalom — moves from confident sleep under armed threat to urgent morning prayers and a plea against a specific accuser named Cush, establishing the book's recurring pattern: honest complaint that resolves into trust rather than denial.

events.title: "I Lay Down and Slept; I Awoke, for Yahweh Sustains Me"
events.detail: Fleeing his own son Absalom with adversaries multiplying against him, David can still sleep soundly and wake unafraid, and a companion evening psalm closes the day the same way: "In peace I will both lie down and sleep, For You alone, O Yahweh, make me to abide in safety."

verses.text: I lay down and slept; I awoke, for Yahweh sustains me. I will not be afraid of ten thousands of people Who all around have set themselves against me.
In peace I will both lie down and sleep, For You alone, O Yahweh, make me to abide in safety.

events.title: Morning Prayer, and "Yahweh Has Heard My Weeping"
events.detail: A prayer offered specifically "in the morning" before deceitful enemies pairs with a psalm of physical and emotional collapse — a bed flooded nightly with tears — that turns decisively the instant David states his confidence: "Yahweh has heard the sound of my weeping."

verses.text: O Yahweh, in the morning, You will hear my voice; In the morning I will order my prayer to You and eagerly watch.
Every night I make my bed swim, I flood my couch with my tears... Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity, For Yahweh has heard the sound of my weeping.

events.title: A Plea Against a False Accuser
events.detail: Naming a specific accuser, Cush the Benjamite, David swears his own innocence under oath and asks God to judge him "according to my righteousness and my integrity," closing with the recurring image of the wicked falling into the very pit they dug for others.

verses.text: He has dug a pit and hollowed it out, And has fallen into the hole which he made. His mischief will return upon his own head.

eras.label: Era III · Psalms 8
eras.name: "What Is Man That You Remember Him?"
eras.dates: A single, soaring hymn steps back from personal complaint to marvel at the created order itself — the moon and stars set against human smallness, yet humanity crowned with glory and given dominion over creation, language the book of Hebrews later applies to Christ's own exaltation.

events.title: Crowned With Glory and Majesty
events.detail: Framed by the identical refrain at its opening and close — "O Yahweh, our Lord, How majestic is Your name in all the earth" — this hymn marvels that a Creator who set the moon and stars in place would also crown mere humanity with glory and give it dominion over the works of His hands.

verses.text: When I see Your heavens, the work of Your fingers, The moon and the stars, which You have established; What is man that You remember him... Yet You have made him a little lower than the angels, And You crown him with glory and majesty!

eras.label: Era IV · Psalms 9-14
eras.name: Refuge for the Oppressed, and "The Fool Has Said in His Heart"
eras.dates: A pair of acrostic psalms on divine justice for the afflicted gives way to shorter prayers of refuge, before the section closes on one of the Psalter's most quoted diagnoses of human nature — repeated twice, almost word for word, within this same short cluster.

events.title: "Yahweh Also Will Be a Stronghold for the Oppressed"
events.detail: A linked pair of acrostic psalms — originally likely one poem — praises Yahweh as an eternal judge who has "not forsaken those who seek You," then turns to lament how the wicked prosper by telling themselves "God has forgotten," closing with a plea that the fatherless and oppressed will finally receive justice.

verses.text: Yahweh also will be a stronghold for the oppressed, A stronghold in times of distress; And those who know Your name will put their trust in You, For You, O Yahweh, have not forsaken those who seek You.

events.title: "In Yahweh I Take Refuge"
events.detail: Against advice to flee like a bird to the mountains, David insists on staying put in trust, since Yahweh's own eyes are already testing "the sons of men" — a confidence paired with a short psalm lamenting a culture of flattering, double-hearted speech.

verses.text: In Yahweh I take refuge; How can you say to my soul, "Flee as a bird to your mountain."

events.title: "How Long, O Yahweh?" and "The Fool Has Said in His Heart, 'There Is No God'"
events.detail: A brief, aching cry of "how long" resolves into trust by its final verse, immediately followed by one of the Bible's most quoted lines about practical atheism — repeated nearly word for word later at Psalm 53 — describing not intellectual denial but moral corruption dressed up as unbelief.

verses.text: How long, O Yahweh? Will You forget me forever?... But I have trusted in Your lovingkindness; My heart shall rejoice in Your salvation.
The wicked fool says in his heart, "There is no God." They act corruptly, they commit abominable deeds; There is no one who does good.

eras.label: Era V · Psalms 15-17
eras.name: Who May Dwell in Your Tent? and "You Will Not Abandon My Soul to Sheol"
eras.dates: A short liturgy naming the ethical qualifications for approaching God's presence leads into one of the Psalter's most quoted resurrection texts — a psalm the apostle Peter applies directly to Christ's resurrection in his first recorded sermon in Acts 2 — and closes with a prayer to awake satisfied by beholding God's own likeness.

events.title: "Who May Sojourn in Your Tent?"
events.detail: In a brief liturgical checklist, the qualifications for approaching Yahweh's presence turn out to be entirely ethical — blameless walking, truthful speech, refusing bribes and usury — rather than ritual, closing with the promise that whoever does these things "will never be shaken."

events.title: "You Will Not Abandon My Soul to Sheol"
events.detail: David's confidence that Yahweh will not "give Your Holy One over to see corruption" becomes, in Peter's Pentecost sermon in Acts 2, direct prophetic evidence for Christ's resurrection, since David himself did in fact die and see decay.

verses.text: For You will not forsake my soul to Sheol; You will not give Your Holy One over to see corruption. You will make known to me the path of life; In Your presence is fullness of joy.

events.title: "I Will Be Satisfied When I Awake With Your Likeness"
events.detail: A prayer for vindication against violent enemies — described as lions lurking to tear their prey — closes on an unusually intimate, almost visionary final line about beholding God's face in righteousness.

verses.text: As for me, I shall behold Your face in righteousness; I will be satisfied with Your likeness when I awake.

eras.label: Era VI · Psalms 18
eras.name: David's Royal Song of Deliverance
eras.dates: A long, theophanic thanksgiving — nearly identical to 2 Samuel 22 — pictures Yahweh descending in storm and earthquake to rescue David from Saul, transforming the king into a warrior who scales walls and crushes enemies, closing with a promise of lovingkindness extended to David's offspring forever.

events.title: "He Bowed the Heavens and Came Down"
events.detail: David's victory song opens with a cascade of images for God as fortress, rock, and shield, before the earth itself shakes and Yahweh descends riding a cherub through darkness and hail to personally draw David out of "many waters."

verses.text: Yahweh is my rock and my fortress and my deliverer, My God, my rock, in whom I take refuge; My shield and the horn of my salvation, my stronghold.
He bowed the heavens and came down With thick darkness under His feet. He rode upon a cherub and flew.

events.title: "You Make My Feet Like Hinds' Feet"
events.detail: David attributes his rescue to his own covenant faithfulness — "According to the cleanness of my hands" — before describing Yahweh personally training him for battle, giving him a warrior's agility and the strength to bend a bow of bronze.

verses.text: He makes my feet like hinds' feet, And sets me upon my high places. He trains my hands for battle, So that my arms can bend a bow of bronze.

events.title: "He Gives Great Salvation to His King"
events.detail: The song closes with David pursuing and crushing every enemy, ruling over nations he had never known, and a final promise that Yahweh's lovingkindness will extend "to David and his seed forever" — a royal promise the Psalter will return to again and again.

verses.text: He gives great salvation to His king, And shows lovingkindness to His anointed, To David and his seed forever.

eras.label: Era VII · Psalms 19-21
eras.name: The Heavens Declare, the Perfect Law, and the King's Joy
eras.dates: Creation and Scripture are named together as twin witnesses to God's glory — the sky preaching wordlessly, the law refreshing the soul — before two short royal psalms pray for the king's victory and celebrate the joy God gives him in return.

events.title: "The Heavens Declare the Glory of God"
events.detail: In one of the Psalter's most celebrated single poems, wordless creation and the LORD's own written law are named as twin, complementary revelations — the sky preaching without speech, the law "restoring the soul" — closing with a prayer that words and thoughts alike would be acceptable to God.

verses.text: The heavens are telling of the glory of God; And the expanse is declaring the work of His hands.
The law of Yahweh is perfect, restoring the soul; The testimony of Yahweh is sure, making wise the simple.
Let the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart Be acceptable in Your sight, O Yahweh, my rock and my Redeemer.

events.title: A Prayer for the King's Victory, and His Resulting Joy
events.detail: A congregational prayer asking Yahweh to answer the king "in the day of distress" is answered directly by its companion psalm, which celebrates the joy and splendor God has actually given him — a request-and-response pair framing kingship as fundamentally dependent on God rather than military strength.

verses.text: Some boast in chariots and some in horses, But we will boast in the name of Yahweh, our God.
O Yahweh, in Your strength the king will be glad, And in Your salvation how greatly he will rejoice!

eras.label: Era VIII · Psalms 22-24
eras.name: The Cry of Dereliction, the Shepherd Psalm, and the King of Glory
eras.dates: Three of the Psalter's most iconic poems stand back to back — the raw cry of abandonment Jesus quotes from the cross, the tender confidence of the Shepherd Psalm, and a processional hymn welcoming the King of Glory through Jerusalem's gates.

events.title: "My God, My God, Why Have You Forsaken Me?"
events.detail: David's opening cry of abandonment — quoted by Jesus word for word on the cross — moves through graphic suffering described with startling precision (pierced hands and feet, divided garments, cast lots) before turning, at verse 22, into confident praise that "all the ends of the earth will remember and turn to Yahweh."

verses.text: My God, my God, why have You forsaken me? Far from my salvation are the words of my groaning.
They pierced my hands and my feet... they cast lots.
All the ends of the earth will remember and turn to Yahweh, And all the families of the nations will worship before You.

events.title: "Yahweh Is My Shepherd; I Shall Not Want"
events.detail: Perhaps the single most familiar psalm in the Bible pictures Yahweh as a shepherd who leads through green pastures and the valley of the shadow of death alike, and as a host who prepares a table even "in the presence of my enemies."

verses.text: Yahweh is my shepherd, I shall not want... Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I fear no evil, for You are with me.
Surely goodness and lovingkindness will pursue me all the days of my life, And I will dwell in the house of Yahweh forever.

events.title: "Who Is This King of Glory?"
events.detail: A processional liturgy — likely sung as the ark entered Jerusalem — asks who may ascend Yahweh's holy hill, answering with an ethical standard of clean hands and a pure heart, before a call-and-response finale demands the city gates lift up for the King of Glory to enter.

verses.text: Lift up your heads, O gates, And be lifted up, O ancient doors, That the King of glory may come in! Who is this King of glory? Yahweh strong and mighty, Yahweh mighty in battle.

eras.label: Era IX · Psalms 25-31
eras.name: Trust, Refuge, and Deliverance
eras.dates: A run of Davidic psalms explores integrity under pressure, waiting on Yahweh's timing, and complete dependence in crisis, closing with the words Jesus himself prays from the cross as his final breath.

events.title: "To You, O Yahweh, I Lift Up My Soul"
events.detail: An acrostic psalm of trust asking to be taught Yahweh's paths pairs with a psalm of self-examination — David inviting God to "test me... and try me" — both grounded in the conviction that integrity, not merely circumstance, is what sustains a person through trouble.

verses.text: To You, O Yahweh, I lift up my soul... Make me know Your ways, O Yahweh; Teach me Your paths.
Test me, O Yahweh, and try me; Refine my mind and my heart.

events.title: "Yahweh Is My Light and My Salvation"
events.detail: Fearless confidence in the face of a besieging army rests on a single, focused desire — to dwell in Yahweh's house and behold His beauty — paired with a companion prayer not to be "dragged away with the wicked," closing on the image of Yahweh as shepherd who "carries them forever."

verses.text: Yahweh is my light and my salvation; Whom shall I fear?... One thing I have asked from Yahweh, that I shall seek: That I may dwell in the house of Yahweh all the days of my life.

events.title: "Ascribe to Yahweh Glory" and "Weeping Lasts for the Night, but Joy Comes in the Morning"
events.detail: A storm theophany pictures Yahweh's voice breaking cedars and stripping forests bare, followed by a dedication psalm whose most quoted line captures the whole book's theology of reversal in a single phrase.

verses.text: The voice of Yahweh is powerful, The voice of Yahweh is full of splendor.
For His anger is but for a moment, His favor is for a lifetime; Weeping may last for the night, But a shout of joy comes in the morning.

events.title: "Into Your Hand I Commit My Spirit"
events.detail: David's prayer of complete dependence under siege — including the line Jesus prays as his own final words from the cross — moves from feeling "like a broken vessel" to renewed courage: "Be strong and let your heart take courage, All you who wait for Yahweh."

verses.text: Into Your hand I commit my spirit; You have ransomed me, O Yahweh, God of truth.
Be strong and let your heart take courage, All you who wait for Yahweh.

eras.label: Era X · Psalms 32-34
eras.name: Forgiveness, and "Taste and See"
eras.dates: A psalm of forgiveness born from David's own guilty silence gives way to a hymn on God's word creating the world, then an acrostic thanksgiving inviting every reader to personally sample the goodness of God for themselves.

events.title: "Blessed Is He Whose Transgression Is Forgiven"
events.detail: David describes the physical toll of concealed guilt — bones wasting away, vitality drained "as with the heat of summer" — reversed the moment he stops hiding it: "I will confess my transgressions to Yahweh; And You forgave the iniquity of my sin."

verses.text: When I kept silent about my sin, my bones wasted away... I said, "I will confess my transgressions to Yahweh;" And You forgave the iniquity of my sin.

events.title: "By the Word of Yahweh the Heavens Were Made"
events.detail: A hymn of pure praise credits creation entirely to divine speech — "He spoke, and it was; He commanded, and it stood" — while insisting that no army or warhorse can substitute for the eye of Yahweh watching over those who fear Him.

verses.text: By the word of Yahweh the heavens were made, And by the breath of His mouth all their host... For He spoke, and it was; He commanded, and it stood.

events.title: "O Taste and See That Yahweh Is Good"
events.detail: Composed, according to its own superscription, after David feigned madness to escape King Abimelech, this acrostic thanksgiving turns personal deliverance into a universal invitation — an invitation the New Testament letter of 1 Peter later quotes directly.

verses.text: O taste and see that Yahweh is good; How blessed is the man who takes refuge in Him!
Yahweh is near to the brokenhearted And saves those who are crushed in spirit.

eras.label: Era XI · Psalms 35-39
eras.name: Imprecatory Prayers, and "Do Not Fret"
eras.dates: A prayer against betrayal by former friends sits alongside meditations on the wicked's self-deception, the Psalter's great wisdom poem on patience toward evildoers, and two raw psalms of physical suffering under what David reads as divine discipline for his own sin.

events.title: "Fight Against Those Who Fight Against Me"
events.detail: David prays urgently for divine intervention against enemies who repaid his own compassion — sackcloth and fasting when they were sick — with mockery once his fortunes turned, closing with a vow to praise God publicly once vindicated.

verses.text: when they were sick, my clothing was sackcloth; I humbled my soul with fasting... I walked about as though it were my friend or brother.

events.title: "Your Lovingkindness Extends to the Heavens" and "Do Not Fret Because of Evildoers"
events.detail: A brief meditation on the wicked man's self-flattering blindness to his own sin opens into towering praise of Yahweh's cosmic lovingkindness, before a long acrostic wisdom psalm delivers the Psalter's clearest counsel on watching the prosperous wicked without envy — patience grounded in the confidence that "the meek will inherit the land," the very words Jesus echoes in the Beatitudes.

verses.text: Your lovingkindness, O Yahweh, is in the heavens, Your faithfulness reaches to the skies.
Do not fret because of evildoers, Be not envious toward doers of unrighteousness... Be still in Yahweh and wait patiently for Him.
But the lowly will inherit the land And will delight themselves in abundant peace.

events.title: Two Psalms of Physical Suffering Under Discipline
events.detail: David describes his own guilt as a physical weight — wounds that "stink and rot" — read as Yahweh's own discipline for sin, paired with a psalm of resolved silence before enemies that dissolves into a meditation on the sheer brevity of human life: "You have made my days as handbreadths."

verses.text: There is no soundness in my flesh because of Your indignation... For my iniquities go over my head.
Yahweh, cause me to know my end And what is the extent of my days... Behold, You have made my days as handbreadths.

eras.label: Era XII · Psalms 40-41
eras.name: Waiting Patiently, and the Betrayer's Bread
eras.dates: Book I closes with a psalm of patient waiting that explicitly reframes obedience over sacrifice — quoted at length in Hebrews as pointing to Christ's own incarnation — followed by a psalm whose description of a trusted friend's betrayal Jesus applies directly to Judas at the Last Supper.

events.title: "I Waited Patiently for Yahweh"
events.detail: David describes being drawn out of "the pit of destruction" and given "a new song," then states a principle the book of Hebrews later reads as messianic prophecy — that God desires obedience over ritual sacrifice, "a body You have prepared for Me."

verses.text: I hoped earnestly for Yahweh; And He inclined to me and heard my cry for help. He brought me up out of the pit of destruction, out of the miry clay.
Sacrifice and meal offering You have not desired; My ears You have opened; Burnt offering and sin offering You have not required.

events.title: "Even My Close Friend... Has Lifted Up His Heel Against Me"
events.detail: Book I's closing psalm on caring for the poor turns personal when David describes betrayal by his own trusted table-companion — language Jesus applies directly to Judas Iscariot at the Last Supper — before Book I ends, as each of the Psalter's five books will, with its own doxology.

verses.text: Even my close friend in whom I trusted, Who ate my bread, Has lifted up his heel against me.
Blessed be Yahweh, the God of Israel, From everlasting to everlasting. Amen and Amen.

eras.label: Era XIII · Psalms 42-43
eras.name: "As the Deer Pants for the Water Brooks"
eras.dates: Book II opens with what was likely originally a single poem, split by later tradition into two psalms sharing an identical refrain — a soul in exile longing for the temple courts it can no longer visit, talking itself back into hope three separate times within the same poem.

events.title: "Why Are You in Despair, O My Soul?"
events.detail: Cut off from the temple and taunted with "Where is your God?", the psalmist's longing is compared to a deer panting for water, and the same refrain of self-address — arguing his own soul back toward hope — repeats three times across what was almost certainly originally one continuous poem.

verses.text: As the deer pants for the water brooks, So my soul pants for You, O God. My soul thirsts for God, for the living God.
Why are you in despair, O my soul?... Wait for God, for I shall still praise Him.

eras.label: Era XIV · Psalms 44-45
eras.name: A National Lament, and a Royal Wedding Song
eras.dates: A communal cry over military defeat — protesting the nation has not actually forsaken the covenant — sits beside a lavish royal wedding song whose opening address to the king as "God" the book of Hebrews later reads as a direct messianic title.

events.title: "We Have Not Forgotten You"
events.detail: Unlike many laments that trace suffering back to Israel's own sin, this communal cry insists the defeat came despite covenant faithfulness — "we have not dealt falsely with Your covenant" — closing with an urgent appeal for God to wake up and act.

verses.text: All this has come upon us, but we have not forgotten You, And we have not dealt falsely with Your covenant... Arouse Yourself, why do You sleep, O Lord?

events.title: "Your Throne, O God, Is Forever and Ever"
events.detail: A wedding song for a royal marriage addresses the king in language of startling elevation — "Your throne, O God, is forever and ever" — a line the New Testament book of Hebrews applies directly to the Son as evidence of his deity.

verses.text: Your throne, O God, is forever and ever; A scepter of uprightness is the scepter of Your kingdom. You have loved righteousness and hated wickedness; Therefore God, Your God, has anointed You.

eras.label: Era XV · Psalms 46-48
eras.name: God Our Refuge, and Zion the Great King's City
eras.dates: One of the Reformation's favorite psalms — the direct inspiration for Luther's "A Mighty Fortress" — pictures God as an unshakeable refuge amid cosmic upheaval, followed by an enthronement hymn and a processional celebration of Jerusalem as the city of the great King.

events.title: "Be Still, and Know That I Am God"
events.detail: Martin Luther's inspiration for "A Mighty Fortress Is Our God" pictures Yahweh as unshakeable refuge even if mountains fall into the heart of the sea, closing on a divine command to stop striving entirely and simply recognize who is in control.

verses.text: God is our refuge and strength, A very present help in trouble. Therefore we will not fear, though the earth should change And though the mountains shake into the heart of the sea.
"Cease striving and know that I am God; I will be exalted among the nations, I will be exalted in the earth."

events.title: "God Reigns Over the Nations", and the City of the Great King
events.detail: A short enthronement hymn calling all peoples to clap and shout gives way to a walking tour of Jerusalem itself — count her towers, consider her ramparts — offered as tangible proof that "this is God, our God forever and ever."

verses.text: God reigns over the nations, God sits on His holy throne.
Walk about Zion and go around her; Count her towers... For this is God, Our God forever and ever; He will guide us over death.

eras.label: Era XVI · Psalms 49-50
eras.name: The Riddle of Wealth and Death, and True Sacrifice
eras.dates: A wisdom psalm on the impossibility of buying one's way out of death gives way to an Asaph psalm in which God himself interrupts formal worship to clarify that he never actually needed the sacrifices — he wanted gratitude and honesty instead.

events.title: "No Man Can Redeem His Brother"
events.detail: A wisdom psalm addressed to "all peoples" observes that no amount of wealth can purchase an exemption from death, since even wise men die and leave their fortunes to others — a riddle resolved only by trusting that "God will redeem my soul from the power of Sheol."

verses.text: Truly, no man can redeem his brother; He cannot give to God a ransom for him... But God will redeem my soul from the power of Sheol, For He will receive me.

events.title: "I Will Not Accept a Bull From Your House"
events.detail: God himself speaks directly, interrupting Israel's formal sacrificial system to clarify he was never actually hungry for burnt offerings — what he wanted all along was thanksgiving, kept vows, and honest living, not ritual performance from people who "cast My words behind you."

verses.text: I shall take no young bull out of your house Nor male goats out of your folds... Offer to God a sacrifice of thanksgiving And pay your vows to the Most High.

eras.label: Era XVII · Psalms 51
eras.name: "Create in Me a Clean Heart, O God"
eras.dates: Confronted by the prophet Nathan after his affair with Bathsheba, David's confession becomes the Psalter's definitive penitential prayer — admitting sin "against You, You only," and asking not merely for pardon but for an entirely renewed inner life.

events.title: "Create in Me a Clean Heart, O God"
events.detail: Written, its superscription says, after Nathan confronted David over Bathsheba, this is the Psalter's deepest confession — acknowledging that sin is ultimately "against You, You only," and asking not just for forgiveness but for a genuinely new heart and a steadfast spirit, since "the sacrifices of God are a broken spirit."

verses.text: Against You, You only, I have sinned And done what is evil in Your sight... Create in me a clean heart, O God, And renew a steadfast spirit within me.
The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; A broken and a contrite heart, O God, You will not despise.

eras.label: Era XVIII · Psalms 52-59
eras.name: David's Psalms From the Years of Saul's Persecution
eras.dates: Eight psalms, several carrying superscriptions naming the exact circumstances — Doeg's betrayal, the Ziphites' report to Saul, the cave, watchers posted at David's own house — trace the years David spent as a hunted fugitive, moving between raw fear and the settled conviction that "God is my stronghold."

events.title: Doeg's Betrayal, and "The Fool Has Said in His Heart" Repeated
events.detail: Named for Doeg the Edomite's betrayal of the priests at Nob, this psalm contrasts a deceitful "mighty man" with David's own image of a flourishing olive tree, paired with an almost word-for-word repetition of Psalm 14's diagnosis of practical atheism as moral corruption rather than honest doubt.

verses.text: But as for me, I am like a green olive tree in the house of God; I trust in the lovingkindness of God forever and ever.
The wicked fool says in his heart, "There is no God," They act corruptly, and commit abominable injustice.

events.title: Betrayed by the Ziphites, and "You Have Kept Count of My Tossings"
events.detail: Betrayed to Saul by the very people of Ziph he had sought refuge among, David's prayers move through strangers turned informants, a close friend's smoother-than-butter treachery, and captivity in Gath, each resolving in trust: "When I am afraid, I will trust in You."

verses.text: it is not an enemy who reproaches me... But it is you, a man my equal, My close companion and my familiar friend.
When I am afraid, I will trust in You... You have taken account of my wanderings; Put my tears in Your bottle. Are they not in Your book?

events.title: Hiding in the Cave, and Watched by Saul's Men
events.detail: Written while hiding from Saul in a cave and while Saul's men watched his own house to kill him, these psalms swing between vivid danger — "My soul is among lions" — and settled resolve, closing on the refrain that becomes David's signature confession under threat: "God is my stronghold."

verses.text: My soul is among lions... My heart is set, O God, my heart is set; I will sing, yes, I will sing praises!
Because of his strength I will watch for You, For God is my stronghold... For God is my stronghold, the God who shows me lovingkindness.

eras.label: Era XIX · Psalms 60-64
eras.name: Prayers From Defeat, and Longing for God
eras.dates: A psalm following a specific military setback against Edom turns quickly to trust, and a cluster of shorter prayers for the king's long life and personal protection culminate in one of the Psalter's most intensely physical expressions of longing for God's presence.

events.title: "O God, You Have Rejected Us", and a Prayer for the King's Long Life
events.detail: Composed after a military setback against Edom despite an earlier victory over Aram, this psalm of national defeat pairs with a personal prayer asking Yahweh to "add days to the king's life" and let him "sit enthroned before God forever."

verses.text: O God, You have rejected us. You have broken us; You have been angry; Oh, restore us... Through God we shall do valiantly, And it is He who will tread down our adversaries.

events.title: "My Soul Thirsts for You, My Flesh Yearns for You"
events.detail: A meditation on waiting "in silence" for God alone as rock and salvation is followed, in the wilderness of Judah, by one of the most physically intense expressions of longing in the whole Psalter — thirst, hunger, and satisfaction all used as metaphors for the presence of God.

verses.text: Surely my soul waits in silence for God; From Him is my salvation. Surely He is my rock and my salvation, My stronghold.
O God, You are my God; I shall seek You earnestly; My soul thirsts for You, my flesh yearns for You, In a dry and weary land without water.

events.title: Protection From Secret Plots
events.detail: A prayer against enemies who "sharpen their tongue like a sword" and plot in secret closes with confidence that God will "shoot them with an arrow" in return — the same weapon imagery turned back on those who wielded it first.

eras.label: Era XX · Psalms 65-68
eras.name: Praise, Harvest, and the God Who Rides Through the Wilderness
eras.dates: A hymn celebrating both answered prayer and agricultural abundance leads into a missionary-minded blessing and a triumphant procession psalm depicting God marching through the wilderness as a warrior-king — the source of the hymn "Let God Arise."

events.title: Praise for Answered Prayer and the Harvest
events.detail: God's answer to prayer is celebrated alongside his provision for the physical world — furrows watered, hills "girded with rejoicing" — before a companion psalm of thanksgiving recalls the exodus itself: "He turned the sea into dry land."

verses.text: You crown the year with Your goodness, And Your paths drip with richness.
He turned the sea into dry land; They passed through the river on foot; There let us be glad in Him!

events.title: "That Your Way May Be Known on the Earth"
events.detail: A short priestly blessing, echoing the Aaronic benediction of Numbers 6, reframes Israel's own blessing as instrumental to a larger, missionary purpose — that all the nations would come to know and praise God too.

verses.text: God be gracious to us and bless us, And cause His face to shine upon us... That Your way may be known on the earth, Your salvation among all nations.

events.title: "Let God Arise, Let His Enemies Be Scattered"
events.detail: A sweeping procession hymn — the direct source of the classic "Let God Arise" — pictures Yahweh as a warrior-king marching through the wilderness at Sinai, father to the fatherless, who "daily bears our burden," and to whom "belong escapes from death" itself.

verses.text: Let God arise, let His enemies be scattered, And let those who hate Him flee before Him.
Blessed be the Lord, who daily bears our burden, The God who is our salvation... And to Yahweh the Lord belong escapes from death.

eras.label: Era XXI · Psalms 69-71
eras.name: Deep Waters, and a Prayer for Old Age
eras.dates: A psalm of drowning distress, heavily quoted throughout the New Testament in connection with Christ's suffering, gives way to a shorter urgent plea and a mature prayer asking specifically not to be abandoned by God in old age.

events.title: "Save Me, O God, for the Waters Have Threatened My Life"
events.detail: One of the most New-Testament-quoted psalms in the whole Psalter describes drowning distress, undeserved reproach for "zeal for Your house," and being offered gall and vinegar — details the Gospels apply directly to Christ's crucifixion — before turning to praise that God "will save Zion."

verses.text: Save me, O God, For the waters have threatened my life. I have sunk in deep clay, and there is no foothold.
For zeal for Your house has consumed me... they also gave me gall for my food And for my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.

events.title: "Do Not Cast Me Off in the Time of Old Age"
events.detail: An urgent, almost identical repetition of Psalm 40's closing plea for quick rescue is followed by a mature believer's prayer — someone who has trusted God "from my youth" — asking specifically not to be forsaken when strength finally fails.

verses.text: Do not cast me off in the time of old age; Do not forsake me when my strength fails... even when I am old and gray, O God, do not forsake me, Until I declare Your strength to this generation.

eras.label: Era XXII · Psalms 72
eras.name: Solomon's Royal Psalm
eras.dates: Book II closes with a psalm attributed to Solomon, praying that the king's reign would embody justice for the poor, dominion "from sea to sea," and universal blessing for every nation — followed by an editorial note marking the formal close of David's collected prayers.

events.title: "May He Have Dominion From Sea to Sea"
events.detail: Attributed to Solomon, this royal psalm prays for a king whose justice specifically benefits the poor and needy, whose reign spreads "from sea to sea" and draws blessing to every nation on earth, closing Book II with both a doxology and a striking editorial note: "The prayers of David, the son of Jesse, are completed."

verses.text: For he will deliver the needy when he cries for help, The afflicted also, and him who has no helper. He will have compassion on the poor and needy.
The prayers of David, the son of Jesse, are completed.

eras.label: Era XXIII · Psalms 73
eras.name: Asaph's Crisis of Faith Resolved
eras.dates: Book III opens with Asaph's honest admission that watching the wicked prosper nearly destroyed his own faith — until stepping into the sanctuary reframed everything, and their apparent security is revealed as standing on ground that could give way at any moment.

events.title: "Until I Came Into the Sanctuary of God"
events.detail: Asaph confesses his feet had "almost slipped" watching arrogant, prosperous wicked people suffer no apparent consequences, a crisis resolved only when entering God's sanctuary reframed their security as standing on slippery ground — leading to one of the Psalter's most personal declarations of devotion.

verses.text: as for me, my feet had almost stumbled... For I was envious of the boastful, I saw the peace of the wicked.
Whom have I in heaven but You? And besides You, I desire nothing on earth. My flesh and my heart fail, But God is the rock of my heart and my portion forever.

eras.label: Era XXIV · Psalms 74-76
eras.name: A Ruined Sanctuary, and God's Terrifying Judgment
eras.dates: A communal lament over the temple's physical destruction — axes and hammers smashing its carved work — appeals to God's ancient victories over chaos, before shorter psalms celebrate divine judgment as something even the proudest king cannot withstand.

events.title: "The Enemy Has Damaged Everything Within the Sanctuary"
events.detail: Describing the temple's literal desecration — carved work smashed with hatchets, the sanctuary set on fire — this lament appeals to Yahweh's ancient cosmic victories, crushing the sea monster Leviathan's heads, as grounds for hoping he can act again now.

verses.text: You divided the sea by Your strength; You broke the heads of the sea monsters in the waters. You crushed the heads of Leviathan.

events.title: "He Puts Down One and Raises Up Another"
events.detail: God himself speaks directly, warning the boastful not to "raise up your horn," before a companion psalm celebrates a specific military victory so total that chariot riders and horses alike "slumbered into a deep sleep" at his rebuke.

verses.text: But God is the Judge; He puts down one and raises up another.
But You, You are fearsome; And who can stand in Your presence when once You are angry?

eras.label: Era XXV · Psalms 77-78
eras.name: Remembering God's Deeds, and Israel's Long History Retold
eras.dates: A personal crisis resolved by deliberately remembering God's past faithfulness during the exodus opens into the Psalter's longest historical psalm — a sweeping, unsparing retelling of Israel's whole wilderness story as one long cycle of miraculous provision met by stubborn rebellion.

events.title: "Then I Remembered Your Deeds of Old"
events.detail: A night of anguished questioning — "Has God forgotten to be gracious?" — is answered not with a new argument but with deliberate memory, recalling the exodus in vivid poetic detail: waters trembling, the earth shaking, "Your footprints were not known."

verses.text: Has God forgotten to be gracious... Then I said, "It is my grief, That the right hand of the Most High has changed." I shall remember the deeds of Yah.

events.title: A History Retold: Manna, Quail, and Rebellion
events.detail: Asaph's long historical psalm begins by declaring its own teaching purpose — passing down "dark sayings of old" so future generations won't repeat the mistakes — then narrates the wilderness generation testing God with complaints even while manna rained from heaven and water gushed from struck rock.

verses.text: in their heart they put God to the test By asking for food according to their desire... Can God prepare a table in the wilderness?

events.title: God's Compassion Despite Rebellion, and the Choice of David
events.detail: The history continues through rejected Shiloh and a God who "awoke as if from sleep," resolving in the deliberate choice of the tribe of Judah and, finally, David himself — taken from tending sheep to shepherding the whole nation "with his skillful hands."

verses.text: He also chose David His servant And took him from the sheepfolds... So he shepherded them according to the integrity of his heart, And led them with his skillful hands.

eras.label: Era XXVI · Psalms 79-83
eras.name: Asaph's Laments Over Israel's Suffering, and a Prayer Against Conspiring Nations
eras.dates: A raw communal lament over Jerusalem's desecration and a shepherd-imagery prayer for restoration lead into psalms confronting corrupt human judges and a coalition of neighboring nations conspiring together against Israel's very existence.

events.title: "O God, the Nations Have Come Into Your Inheritance"
events.detail: Jerusalem's desecration and unburied dead prompt an urgent plea for vengeance and atonement, paired with a psalm picturing Israel as a vine God once transplanted from Egypt, now broken down and devoured — its refrain repeated three times: "restore us... that we might be saved."

verses.text: O God, restore us And cause Your face to shine upon us, that we would be saved.

events.title: "Oh That My People Would Listen to Me!"
events.detail: God's own lament over Israel's stubbornness — "I released them over to the stubbornness of their heart" — is followed by a striking scene of God himself presiding over a divine council of unjust "gods," sentencing them to die like mere men for failing the poor and orphan.

verses.text: My people did not listen to My voice... So I released them over to the stubbornness of their heart... Oh that My people would listen to Me!
I said, "You are gods... Nevertheless you will die like men."

events.title: A Coalition of Nations Conspires Against Israel
events.detail: Naming ten specific hostile nations who "conspired together with one heart" to erase Israel's very name from memory, this prayer asks God to scatter them like chaff and whirling dust, so that they would finally "know that You alone... are the Most High over all the earth."

verses.text: "Come, and let us wipe them out as a nation, That the name of Israel be remembered no more." For they have conspired together with one heart.

eras.label: Era XXVII · Psalms 84-85
eras.name: Longing for the Courts of the LORD, and Restoration Hoped For
eras.dates: A Korahite pilgrim psalm expresses some of the Psalter's warmest longing for temple worship, envying even the birds that nest at the altar, followed by a prayer that the same restoration once given the land would come again.

events.title: "How Lovely Are Your Dwelling Places"
events.detail: A pilgrim's longing for the temple courts is expressed with unusual tenderness — even envying the sparrow that has found a home near the altar — culminating in one of the Psalter's most quoted lines about the sheer worth of God's presence.

verses.text: My soul has longed and even fainted for the courts of Yahweh... For better is a day in Your courts than a thousand elsewhere.

events.title: "Lovingkindness and Truth Have Met Together"
events.detail: Recalling a past restoration of Israel's fortunes, this prayer asks for it to happen again, resolving into one of the most quoted lines in the whole Psalter about the reconciling meeting point of God's own character: "Righteousness and peace have kissed each other."

verses.text: Lovingkindness and truth have met together; Righteousness and peace have kissed each other.

eras.label: Era XXVIII · Psalms 86-89
eras.name: David's Prayer, Zion the Mother of Nations, a Dark Psalm, and the Davidic Covenant
eras.dates: A rare Davidic psalm within Book III's mostly Asaph and Korahite collection leads into a striking vision of Zion as spiritual mother to foreign nations, the Psalter's single darkest, most unresolved lament, and finally a long meditation on the Davidic covenant that celebrates God's promise to David before lamenting its apparent, present-day collapse.

events.title: "You, Lord, Are Good, and by Nature Forgiving"
events.detail: One of only two Davidic psalms in Book III's mostly Asaph-and-Korah collection prays with unusual directness for an undivided heart, resting its whole appeal on God's revealed character as "compassionate and gracious, Slow to anger and abundant in lovingkindness."

verses.text: Teach me Your way, O Yahweh; I will walk in Your truth; Unite my heart to fear Your name... You, O Lord, are a God compassionate and gracious.

events.title: Zion, Mother of Nations, and the Psalter's Darkest Lament
events.detail: A short, striking vision pictures foreign nations — even historic enemies like Babylon and Egypt — one day counted as native-born citizens of Zion, immediately followed by the single bleakest psalm in the whole book, a lament that reaches its final line still unresolved: "my acquaintances are in darkness."

verses.text: "I shall mention Rahab and Babylon among those who know Me"... But of Zion it shall be said, "This one and that one were born in her."
You have removed lover and friend far from me; My acquaintances are in darkness.

events.title: The Davidic Covenant Celebrated, Then Lamented
events.detail: Ethan's long psalm opens in soaring praise of God's unbreakable covenant with David — "I will not lie to David" — before pivoting into raw complaint that the covenant now appears broken: the anointed king's crown "profaned to the ground." Book III closes here, its doxology sounding more like a hopeful assertion than a resolved celebration.

verses.text: My covenant I will not profane, Nor will I alter what comes forth from My lips. Once I have sworn by My holiness; I will not lie to David.
You have cast off and rejected, You have been full of wrath against Your anointed... How long, O Yahweh? Will You hide Yourself forever?

eras.label: Era XXIX · Psalms 90-91
eras.name: Moses' Prayer, and the Shelter of the Most High
eras.dates: Book IV answers Book III's unresolved crisis by reaching back to the Psalter's oldest voice — Moses himself — meditating on human frailty against God's eternity, before an anonymous psalm of protection promises complete safety under God's wings, later quoted by Satan himself in tempting Christ.

events.title: "Teach Us to Number Our Days"
events.detail: Attributed to Moses and likely the Psalter's oldest composition, this psalm meditates on the vast gulf between human life — over almost "like a sigh" — and a God for whom a thousand years pass like a single watch in the night, praying for wisdom to make each day count.

verses.text: For a thousand years in Your sight Are like yesterday when it passes by, Or as a watch in the night.
So teach us to number our days, That we may present to You a heart of wisdom.

events.title: "He Who Abides in the Shelter of the Most High"
events.detail: A sweeping promise of divine protection — pestilence, terror, and lions all rendered harmless — includes the very verses about angelic protection that Satan later quotes, twisted out of context, when tempting Jesus in the wilderness.

verses.text: He who abides in the shelter of the Most High Will abide in the shadow of the Almighty... He will cover you with His pinions, And under His wings you will take refuge.
For He will command His angels concerning you, To guard you in all your ways. On their hands they will bear you up.

eras.label: Era XXX · Psalms 92-94
eras.name: Sabbath Praise, and "Shall the Throne of Destruction Be Allied With You?"
eras.dates: A psalm designated specifically for Sabbath worship and an enthronement hymn celebrating God's unshakeable reign give way to a sharp cry for justice, asking pointedly whether corrupt rulers who legislate oppression can really claim any alliance with God at all.

events.title: A Sabbath Song, and "Yahweh Reigns"
events.detail: Specifically composed "for the Sabbath day," this psalm contrasts the wicked's brief, grass-like flourishing with the righteous "planted in the house of Yahweh," paired with a short, majestic hymn on Yahweh's throne established "from of old."

verses.text: The righteous man will flourish like the palm tree, He will grow like a cedar in Lebanon. Planted in the house of Yahweh, They will flourish in the courts of our God.
Yahweh reigns, He is clothed with majesty... Your throne is established from of old; You are from everlasting.

events.title: "Shall a Throne of Destruction Be Allied With You?"
events.detail: A cry against corrupt rulers who "crush Your people" while claiming legal legitimacy poses a pointed rhetorical challenge — can injustice codified into law really claim any alliance with a righteous God? — resolving in confidence that Yahweh himself remains "the rock of my refuge."

verses.text: Can a throne of destruction be allied with You, One which forms trouble by statute?

eras.label: Era XXXI · Psalms 95-100
eras.name: The Enthronement Psalms: "O Come, Let Us Worship"
eras.dates: Six psalms in a row declare, in varied language, the same central claim — Yahweh reigns as King over all the earth — inviting universal worship while soberly warning against repeating the wilderness generation's hardened hearts.

events.title: "O Come, Let Us Worship and Bow Down"
events.detail: An invitation to worship shifts abruptly into warning, recalling the wilderness generation who "tried Me" at Meribah despite having "seen My work," paired with a missionary-minded call for all the earth, not just Israel, to sing Yahweh "a new song."

verses.text: Come, let us worship and bow down, Let us kneel before Yahweh our Maker... Do not harden your hearts, as at Meribah.
Sing to Yahweh a new song; Sing to Yahweh, all the earth... Recount His glory among the nations.

events.title: "Yahweh Reigns", and a New Song of Salvation
events.detail: Fire and lightning accompany Yahweh's reign as "the mountains melt like wax," while a companion psalm imagines the sea roaring and rivers clapping their hands — all creation personified as an audience for God's coming judgment of the world.

verses.text: Let the rivers clap their hands, Let the mountains sing together for joy Before Yahweh, for He is coming to judge the earth.

events.title: "Yahweh Reigns; Let the Peoples Tremble", and "Make a Loud Shout"
events.detail: A final, more solemn enthronement psalm recalling Moses, Aaron, and Samuel as models of prayer answered gives way to the short, joyful Psalm 100 — likely the most familiar call to worship in the whole Psalter, still sung today as the Old Hundredth.

verses.text: Make a loud shout to Yahweh, all the earth. Serve Yahweh with gladness... Know that Yahweh, He is God; It is He who has made us, and not we ourselves.

eras.label: Era XXXII · Psalms 101-103
eras.name: A King's Vow of Integrity, a Cry From Affliction, and "Bless Yahweh, O My Soul"
eras.dates: A royal vow to rule with personal integrity precedes one of the Psalter's most physically vivid laments — likened to a lonely bird on a rooftop — before the section closes with one of its warmest, most quoted hymns of praise for God's fatherly compassion.

events.title: A King's Vow of Personal Integrity
events.detail: David vows to run his own household and administration on strict ethical standards — no deceit, no slander tolerated near him — modeling the kind of personal integrity the rest of the Psalter repeatedly asks God for in others.

verses.text: I will consider the way of the blameless... I will set no vile thing before my eyes; I hate the work of those who fall away.

events.title: "I Resemble a Pelican of the Wilderness"
events.detail: One of the Psalter's most vivid pictures of isolation and physical suffering — likened to a lonely bird, ashes eaten like bread — turns toward hope by recalling Yahweh's eternal permanence against human transience, a contrast the New Testament book of Hebrews applies directly to Christ's own unchanging nature.

verses.text: I resemble a pelican of the wilderness; I have become like an owl of the waste places. I lie awake, I have become like a lonely bird on a roof.
But You are the same, And Your years will not come to an end.

events.title: "Bless Yahweh, O My Soul"
events.detail: One of the Psalter's warmest and most quoted hymns catalogs God's benefits — forgiveness, healing, compassion "as a father has compassion on his children" — closing on the image of God's mercy stretching "as far as the east is from the west."

verses.text: as high as the heavens are above the earth, So great is His lovingkindness... As far as the east is from the west, So far has He removed our transgressions... As a father has compassion on his children, So Yahweh has compassion on those who fear Him.

eras.label: Era XXXIII · Psalms 104-106
eras.name: A Hymn to Creation, and Israel's History Retold Twice
eras.dates: A sweeping creation hymn celebrating every layer of the natural world gives way to two companion historical psalms — one retelling Israel's story as a record of God's faithfulness, the other retelling the identical history as a record of Israel's own repeated rebellion, closing Book IV with its own doxology.

events.title: "O Yahweh, How Manifold Are Your Works!"
events.detail: Following creation roughly in the order of Genesis 1, this hymn moves from light and sky through mountains, springs, and wild animals to a closing celebration of Leviathan, the great sea creature God "formed to play" in the ocean.

verses.text: How numerous are Your works, O Yahweh! In wisdom You have made them all; The earth is full of Your possessions.
There the ships move along, And Leviathan, which You have formed to play in it.

events.title: Israel's History as a Record of God's Faithfulness
events.detail: The same wilderness history covered elsewhere in the Psalter is retold here entirely from the angle of divine faithfulness — Joseph's rise from slavery, the plagues, the exodus — with no mention at all of Israel's own rebellion, a deliberately one-sided companion to the psalm that follows it.

verses.text: He has remembered His covenant forever, The word which He commanded for a thousand generations.

events.title: Israel's History as a Record of Its Own Rebellion
events.detail: The identical history retold in Psalm 105 is recast here as a catalogue of repeated failure — the golden calf, craving meat, Baal-peor — yet God's covenant faithfulness still wins the last word, closing Book IV with a doxology and communal "Amen."

verses.text: We have sinned with our fathers, We have committed iniquity, we have acted wickedly. Our fathers in Egypt did not consider Your wondrous deeds.
Blessed be Yahweh, the God of Israel, From everlasting to everlasting. And let all the people say, "Amen." Praise Yah!

eras.label: Era XXXIV · Psalms 107
eras.name: The Redeemed Give Thanks: Four Scenes of Deliverance
eras.dates: Book V opens with a carefully structured hymn presenting four distinct scenes of distress and rescue — wandering desert travelers, shackled prisoners, the deathly sick, and storm-tossed sailors — each resolving with the identical refrain of thanksgiving.

events.title: Four Scenes of Distress and Rescue
events.detail: In a deliberately structured hymn, four separate groups — lost desert wanderers, shackled prisoners, the dangerously sick, and sailors caught in a violent storm — each cry out to Yahweh in trouble and are each rescued, with the identical refrain repeated after every scene: "Let them give thanks to Yahweh for His lovingkindness."

verses.text: Those who go down to the sea in ships... He caused the storm to stand still, So that its waves were hushed.
Let them give thanks to Yahweh for His lovingkindness, And for His wondrous deeds to the sons of men!

eras.label: Era XXXV · Psalms 108-110
eras.name: A Battle Song, a Plea Against Slander, and "Yahweh Says to My Lord"
eras.dates: A composite psalm assembled from earlier material precedes one of the Psalter's harshest imprecatory prayers against a slanderous accuser, before Book V's opening section climaxes with the single most New-Testament-quoted psalm in the entire Bible.

events.title: A Battle Song Assembled From Earlier Psalms
events.detail: Combining material from Psalm 57 and Psalm 60 almost verbatim, this psalm reuses earlier praise and lament to form a fresh prayer for victory, closing with confidence that "through God we shall do valiantly."

events.title: A Prayer Against a Slanderous Accuser
events.detail: One of the Psalter's harshest imprecatory prayers responds to false accusation with an extended curse, asking that the accuser's own children be orphaned and his memory blotted out — before resolving, as these prayers usually do, into trust that Yahweh "stands at the right hand of the needy."

verses.text: In return for my love they accuse me; But I am in prayer. Thus they have set upon me evil for good And hatred for my love.
For He stands at the right hand of the needy, To save him from those who judge his soul.

events.title: "Yahweh Says to My Lord: Sit at My Right Hand"
events.detail: The single most quoted psalm in the entire New Testament opens with Yahweh addressing David's own "Lord" as a co-regent seated at his right hand, and names him "a priest forever According to the order of Melchizedek" — a text Jesus himself cites to challenge the Pharisees, and the book of Hebrews develops at length.

verses.text: Yahweh says to my Lord: "Sit at My right hand Until I put Your enemies as a footstool for Your feet."
Yahweh has sworn and will not change His mind, "You are a priest forever According to the order of Melchizedek."

eras.label: Era XXXVI · Psalms 111-118
eras.name: The Egyptian Hallel
eras.dates: A cluster of praise psalms traditionally recited at Passover — the "Egyptian Hallel" — moves through twin acrostics on God's works, a mockery of lifeless idols, thanksgiving for rescue from death, the shortest chapter in the whole Bible, and closes on the psalm every Gospel writer quotes concerning the stone the builders rejected.

events.title: Twin Acrostics on Yahweh's Works and the Righteous Man's Blessing
events.detail: Two matching acrostic psalms — one praising Yahweh's own great works, the other describing the blessed life of the person who fears Him — share the identical opening line, "Praise Yah," and the same closing theme, that both God's righteousness and the righteous person's own "stand forever."

verses.text: The fear of Yahweh is the beginning of wisdom; Good insight belongs to all those who do His commandments.
How blessed is the man who fears Yahweh, Who greatly delights in His commandments.

events.title: Lifting the Poor, Trembling at the Exodus, and Mocking Idols
events.detail: Praise for a God who "raises the poor from the dust" opens the traditional Passover Hallel proper, moving through a vivid poem picturing mountains skipping like rams at the exodus, then a sharp satire of idols that have mouths but cannot speak and eyes but cannot see.

verses.text: Who raises the poor from the dust And lifts high the needy from the ash heap.
Their idols are silver and gold, The work of man's hands. They have mouths, but they do not speak; They have eyes, but they do not see.

events.title: Rescue From Death, and the Bible's Shortest Chapter
events.detail: Personal thanksgiving for being rescued from the very "cords of death" leads into the shortest chapter in the entire Bible — just two verses — yet one that reaches beyond Israel entirely, calling "all nations" to praise Yahweh.

verses.text: The cords of death encompassed me And the distresses of Sheol found me... Then I called upon the name of Yahweh.
Praise Yahweh, all nations; Laud Him, all peoples! For His lovingkindness prevails over us, And the truth of Yahweh is everlasting.

events.title: "The Stone Which the Builders Rejected"
events.detail: Closing the Hallel, this psalm of thanksgiving includes the line every Gospel writer quotes concerning Jesus's rejection by Israel's own religious leaders — a rejected stone that becomes, unexpectedly, the very cornerstone of the building.

verses.text: The stone which the builders rejected Has become the chief corner stone. This is from Yahweh; It is marvelous in our eyes.
This is the day which Yahweh has made; Let us rejoice and be glad in it.

eras.label: Era XXXVII · Psalms 119
eras.name: The Great Acrostic on God's Law
eras.dates: The longest chapter in the entire Bible is a massive, twenty-two-stanza acrostic — one stanza per letter of the Hebrew alphabet, eight verses each — meditating relentlessly on the goodness of God's law from every conceivable angle: as lamp, as delight, as comfort in affliction, as sweeter than honey.

events.title: Aleph Through Vav: "How Can a Young Man Keep His Way Pure?"
events.detail: The acrostic's opening third establishes its central question and answer — how can anyone stay morally clean in a fallen world? — by keeping God's word treasured in the heart, promising to run in the path of God's commandments once God "enlarges" the heart to receive them.

verses.text: How can a young man keep his way pure? By keeping it according to Your word... Your word I have treasured in my heart, That I may not sin against You.

events.title: Zayin Through Kaph: Comfort in Affliction
events.detail: The middle stanzas turn to suffering directly, insisting that affliction itself became instructive — "It is good for me that I was afflicted, That I may learn Your statutes" — even while enemies dig pits and smear the psalmist with lies.

verses.text: It is good for me that I was afflicted, That I may learn Your statutes.
My soul fails with longing for Your salvation; I wait for Your word.

events.title: Lamedh Through Ayin: "Your Word Is a Lamp to My Feet"
events.detail: The acrostic's most quoted single line appears here, alongside a striking confession of how God's law has made the psalmist wiser than his own teachers and elders — knowledge measured not in years but in sustained attention to a single source.

verses.text: Your word is a lamp to my feet And a light to my path.
How sweet is Your word to my taste! Sweeter than honey to my mouth!

events.title: Tsadhe Through Tav: A Closing Confession
events.detail: The acrostic's final movement affirms God's righteousness as "an everlasting righteousness" amid ongoing persecution, before ending on a surprisingly vulnerable final line — not a triumphant close, but an admission of continued need for rescue.

verses.text: The sum of Your word is truth, And every one of Your righteous judgments is everlasting.
I have wandered off like a lost sheep; search for Your slave, For I have not forgotten Your commandments.

eras.label: Era XXXVIII · Psalms 120-134
eras.name: The Songs of Ascent
eras.dates: Fifteen short psalms, traditionally sung by pilgrims climbing the road to Jerusalem for the great festivals, trace an actual journey — distress in a foreign land, help arriving "from the hills," arrival at the temple gates, and finally the night watchmen blessing Yahweh from within the sanctuary itself.

events.title: Pilgrims Set Out: "I Lift Up My Eyes to the Hills"
events.detail: The journey begins in exile — "Woe is me, for I sojourn in Meshech" — before the collection's most beloved single psalm asks where help will come from and answers immediately: from Yahweh, "who made heaven and earth," celebrated further by pilgrims already standing within Jerusalem's own gates.

verses.text: I will lift up my eyes to the mountains; From where shall my help come? My help comes from Yahweh, Who made heaven and earth.
I was glad when they said to me, "Let us go to the house of Yahweh." Our feet are standing Within your gates, O Jerusalem.

events.title: "Unless Yahweh Builds the House"
events.detail: The pilgrim collection turns to trust and community — Zion as an unshakeable mountain, God's blessing on ordinary family life, children as "an inheritance of Yahweh" — with the famous reminder that even a well-built house or a wide-awake watchman accomplishes nothing without God's own hand in it.

verses.text: Unless Yahweh builds the house, They labor in vain who build it; Unless Yahweh watches the city, The watchman keeps awake in vain.
How blessed is everyone who fears Yahweh, Who walks in His ways.

events.title: "Out of the Depths", Brothers in Unity, and the Watchmen's Night Blessing
events.detail: The pilgrimage nears its end with one of the Psalter's most quoted cries from despair, a short psalm celebrating the sheer goodness of family unity, and finally the collection's quiet closing scene — temple watchmen blessing Yahweh together by night, having completed the ascent.

verses.text: Out of the depths I called to You, O Yahweh... If You should keep iniquities, O Yah, O Lord, who could stand? But with You there is forgiveness.
Behold, how good and how pleasant it is For brothers to dwell together in unity!
Behold, bless Yahweh, all you slaves of Yahweh, Who stand in the house of Yahweh by night!

eras.label: Era XXXIX · Psalms 135-137
eras.name: Praise for the Exodus, and "By the Rivers of Babylon"
eras.dates: A hymn recounting the exodus and conquest as proof of Yahweh's incomparable power gives way to its own companion litany — the same historical highlights repeated twenty-six times with the identical refrain — before the collection turns to the Psalter's rawest single expression of exile grief.

events.title: Praise for the Exodus and Conquest, With a 26-Fold Refrain
events.detail: A historical hymn celebrating Yahweh's incomparable greatness over "all gods" is followed by its own companion, a litany in which nearly every one of its twenty-six verses closes with the same repeated refrain: "For His lovingkindness endures forever."

verses.text: I know that Yahweh is great And that our Lord is greater than all gods. Whatever Yahweh pleases, He does.
Give thanks to Yahweh, for He is good, For His lovingkindness endures forever.

events.title: "By the Rivers of Babylon, There We Sat and Wept"
events.detail: The Psalter's rawest single expression of exile grief pictures captors demanding songs of joy from a grieving, harp-hanging people, closing on lines so violently raw — a wish for Babylon's infants dashed against rocks — that they remain among the most difficult verses in the entire Bible to read aloud.

verses.text: By the rivers of Babylon, There we sat and also wept, When we remembered Zion.
If I forget you, O Jerusalem, May my right hand forget her skill. May my tongue cling to the roof of my mouth If I do not remember you.

eras.label: Era XL · Psalms 138-140
eras.name: Thanksgiving, "You Have Searched Me and Known Me," and a Prayer Against Evil Men
eras.dates: A psalm of personal thanksgiving for answered prayer sits beside one of Scripture's most intimate meditations on being fully known by God — from the womb to the farthest sea — before the section closes with an urgent plea against violent, scheming enemies.

events.title: "On the Day I Called, You Answered Me"
events.detail: A straightforward psalm of thanksgiving notes that even "all the kings of the earth" will one day give God thanks, resting confidently on the promise that Yahweh "will accomplish what concerns me."

events.title: "O Yahweh, You Have Searched Me and Known Me"
events.detail: One of the most personally intimate psalms in the whole Psalter traces God's presence from before birth — "You wove me in my mother's womb" — to the farthest reaches of sea and sky, closing with an invitation for God to search the heart for anything "hurtful" still hidden there.

verses.text: For You formed my inward parts; You wove me in my mother's womb. I will give thanks to You, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made.
Search me, O God, and know my heart; Try me and know my anxious thoughts; And see if there be any hurtful way in me.

events.title: "Rescue Me, O Yahweh, From Evil Men"
events.detail: A prayer for protection from violent men who "sharpen their tongues as a serpent" closes with quiet confidence that Yahweh personally "will maintain the cause for the afflicted."

eras.label: Era XLI · Psalms 141-144
eras.name: Evening Prayer, a Cry From Prison, and a King's Prayer for Victory
eras.dates: A prayer offered like incense at evening and a psalm crying out from what feels like imprisonment give way to an urgent plea for rescue and a king's own martial prayer, celebrating the God who trains hands for war and blesses ordinary, peaceful abundance in the very next breath.

events.title: "Let My Prayer Be Counted as Incense"
events.detail: An evening prayer asking God to guard the mouth from evil speech pairs with a psalm of complete isolation — "there is no one who regards me" — crying out from what feels like a literal prison for release, so the psalmist can "give thanks to Your name."

verses.text: May my prayer be established as incense before You; The lifting up of my hands as the evening offering.
Bring my soul out of prison, To give thanks to Your name.

events.title: "Teach Me to Do Your Will", and a King's Prayer for Victory
events.detail: An urgent plea for guidance and rescue — "no one living is righteous in Your sight" — is followed by David's own martial prayer, praising Yahweh who "trains my hands for war," before closing unexpectedly on the peaceful abundance of full granaries and thriving children.

verses.text: do not enter into judgment with Your slave, For no one living is righteous in Your sight.
Blessed be Yahweh, my rock, Who trains my hands for war, My fingers for battle.

eras.label: Era XLII · Psalms 145-150
eras.name: The Final Hallel: Praise Crescendo to the Book's Close
eras.dates: The Psalter's final movement abandons lament almost entirely, building through David's own acrostic praise, a celebration of God's care for the oppressed and hungry, a hymn to creation's obedience, and finally five short psalms whose only theme, repeated with mounting intensity, is pure praise — closing on the command for everything that breathes to praise Yahweh.

events.title: David's Acrostic Praise, and "Happy Is He Whose Help Is the God of Jacob"
events.detail: David's own final acrostic psalm celebrates a God "gracious and compassionate" to all his works, followed immediately by a psalm warning against trusting mortal "nobles" whose plans die with them, in favor of the God who executes justice for the oppressed and feeds the hungry.

verses.text: Yahweh is gracious and compassionate; Slow to anger and great in lovingkindness. Yahweh is good to all, And His compassions are over all His works.
How blessed is he whose help is the God of Jacob, Whose hope is in Yahweh his God... Who does justice for the oppressed; Who gives food to the hungry.

events.title: "He Heals the Brokenhearted", and All Creation Commanded to Praise
events.detail: A psalm celebrating God's care for both the brokenhearted and the stars by name gives way to a sweeping roll call commanding every layer of creation — sun, moon, sea monsters, fruit trees, kings, and children alike — to praise Yahweh's name together.

verses.text: He is the One who heals the brokenhearted And who binds up their wounds, Who counts the number of the stars; He gives names to all of them.
Praise Him, sun and moon... Kings of the earth and all peoples... Both choice men as well as virgins; The old with the young.

events.title: "Let Everything That Has Breath Praise Yahweh"
events.detail: The Psalter's final two psalms close the entire book on an unbroken crescendo of praise — dancing, tambourines, every instrument imaginable — ending on the single most quoted command in the whole Psalter, its final word an instruction to every living thing without exception.

verses.text: Praise Him with trumpet blast; Praise Him with harp and lyre. Praise Him with tambourine and dancing; Praise Him with stringed instruments and pipe. Praise Him with resounding cymbals; Praise Him with clashing cymbals.
Let everything that has breath praise Yah. Praise Yah!
